entries.subject: Two-person crosscut saw with two vertical wooden handles and one subordinate felling axe, an organized forestry tool group.
entries.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset: ONE original TECHNOLOGY invention icon for the 1776 Age of Revolutions Victoria 3 mod, not a flat production-method pictogram and not a building icon.
Style: compact hand-painted volumetric object illustration matching vanilla Victoria 3 technology art. Broad readable masses, restrained matte brushed grain, natural distinct material colors, soft upper-left illumination and darker undersides. Not photorealism, glossy CGI, flat vector, embossed gold badge, tiny building or landscape.
Composition: one dominant object or one coherent working apparatus, at most one meaningful subordinate accessory. Modest elevated three-quarter view, square canvas at least 1024 pixels, centered whole object with generous genuine transparent margins, readable at 48 and 64 pixels. Do not crop extremities.
Background: genuine transparent alpha outside the object and through exterior gaps. No painted black, white or checkerboard backdrop; no ground, floor, ground cast shadow, frame, circle, medallion, room or scenery. Object contact shading is allowed.
Natural material palette: wood brown, iron warm neutral grey, stone warm grey, pottery terracotta; NO global blue/teal color cast, no uniform sepia filter. No letters, numbers, scales, labels, arrows, logos, watermark, people or hands.
Historically informed conceptual illustration, not a scale-certified reconstruction. No modern motors, electricity, plastic or fantasy machinery. No display of finished goods in the foreground.
Primary request: ORGANIZED FORESTRY, represented by a late eighteenth-century TWO-PERSON CROSSCUT SAW as the dominant tool, paired with ONE modest felling axe as the only accessory.
The saw is one long moderately broad steel blade with a gently arched smooth upper spine, a continuous lower cutting edge carrying SIMPLE REGULAR TRIANGULAR PEG TEETH. No alternate huge raker teeth or chainsaw chain. Blade warm-neutral charcoal grey with restrained pale steel edges, no blue shine.
At EACH END, a short forged iron tang is securely riveted to the blade and turns upward to hold one plain straight ash-wood vertical cylindrical handle. Exactly TWO handles, one at each end; no third handle, bow frame, brace or horizontal grip. The wood grips extend upward perpendicular to the length of the blade and remain visibly attached.
Arrange the saw diagonally from lower-left to upper-right to fill the square. Compress the depiction modestly for icon readability while retaining a long saw, generous handles and blade broad enough to read at 48 pixels. Keep the entire blade, both handles and teeth intact.
ONE small traditional felling axe rests diagonally behind the saw, a short brown wooden haft firmly inserted through the eye of one dark iron head, axe blade facing outward left. It crosses only the central part of the saw and must not obscure either handle or the characteristic saw teeth. The saw remains clearly dominant; the axe is a subordinate forestry cue.
The principle and attachment shapes are informed by Colonial Williamsburg's Thomas Bernard crosscut saw dated 1775–1800. Depict a complete usable conceptual tool, not the museum label or its display surface.
No tree, log pile, stump, forest landscape, finished boards, timber building, tape measure, caliper, mechanized saw, ribbon or extra props.

entries.subject: One working rotary hand-quern, two stone discs with a central feed eye and a distinct off-centre wooden handle.
entries.prompt:

Style: compact hand-painted volumetric object illustration matching vanilla Victoria 3 technology art. Not photorealism, glossy CGI, flat vector, embossed gold badge, tiny building or landscape.

Historically informed conceptual illustration, not a scale-certified reconstruction. No modern motors, electricity, plastic or fantasy machinery. No display of finished goods in the foreground.
Primary request: TRADITIONAL FOOD PROCESSING, represented by ONE simple WORKING ROTARY HAND-QUERN for milling grain. The actual grinding apparatus is the whole subject, not a food still life.
Two thick round stone discs stacked concentrically: a broad stationary lower stone and a slightly smaller rotating upper stone resting directly on it. Both stone masses in warm neutral grey sandstone with restrained speckled mineral grain, wear softened but not crumbling ruins. Broad simple rim and thick side faces for small-size legibility.
The upper stone has a shallow bowl-shaped hopper sloping into ONE clearly visible central circular feed eye. A few warm tan grain kernels lie INSIDE the hopper only, not outside in a pile. The central eye remains a visibly hollow opening, NOT filled by a handle or shaft.
ONE stout straight brown wooden turning handle stands upright in a separate socket NEAR THE OUTER EDGE of the upper stone, on a small integral stone lug at the back-right circumference. The handle is firmly inserted in this offset socket. Make the peripheral handle and central feed eye spatially distinct. Never put the turning handle in the central hole.
The lower and upper stones make direct physical contact along their grinding surfaces; a fine dark seam is visible between them, not a large empty space or hovering top stone. Modest elevated three-quarter perspective exposes the feed hopper, handle socket and both disc side walls.
Reference: Cotswold Archaeology's Roman upper quernstone documents a central eye, shallow hopper and a peripheral lug for a vertical handle. This icon is a complete conceptual reconstruction of the ancient milling principle, NOT an assertion that that excavated fragment dates to 1776.
No flour sack, bread, butter, meat, finished food, foreground wheat stalks, table, base pedestal, fireplace, oven, building, gear train, crank at the central hole, modern mill, decorative ring, lettering or extra accessories.

entries.subject: A bright white crystallized sugarloaf and its matching empty terracotta conical refining mould, a compact process-and-result concept.
entries.prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit.
Asset type: ONE TECHNOLOGY invention icon for Victoria 3 / 1776 Age of Revolutions, a painted volumetric concept with genuine transparent alpha.
Input images: Image 1 is the old sugar refining icon to REPLACE in subject, not preserve in composition. Images 2 and 3 are native Victoria 3 TECHNOLOGY STYLE REFERENCES ONLY; do not insert their drill, sack, seedling, outlines or blue accents.
Primary request: The old stacked clay cone and jar is not readable as SUGAR REFINING. Completely replace that apparatus with a bright white, clearly crystallized SUGARLOAF as the dominant subject and its matching EMPTY CONICAL TERRACOTTA REFINING MOULD as the sole meaningful accessory. These two matching forms communicate the forming and crystallization of refined sugar, not two ordinary pots.
Main subject: ONE solid unwrapped historical cone-shaped sugarloaf, broad circular flat base, moderately tall tapering body and softly rounded narrow tip, standing upright in a modest three-quarter view. Matte clean near-white crystalline sugar, fine restrained granules and a few tiny irregular crystal facets, not cloth, paper, stone, chalk, ice, snow, candle or dessert. The cone is entirely visible and clearly dominant in scale and contrast.
Accessory: ONE open, EMPTY reddish terracotta conical mould positioned close beside and slightly behind the sugarloaf, tilted so its wide open elliptical mouth and dark hollow interior are plainly visible. Its narrow closed tip points away. The internal taper, usable depth and opening diameter plausibly match the FULL sugarloaf standing beside it: the loaf could have been formed inside this mould. Thick simple rim, smooth gently worn earthenware sides. This is an intact deep conical mould, not a terracotta flower pot with flat bottom, a small bowl, half-shell, ladle or funnel with a tube.
Compact coherent two-object group: large white loaf plus one closely adjacent mould. No jar underneath, no extra pots, no third object. Clear non-overlapping essential silhouettes. The mould explains the technique; the bright crystal cone makes SUGAR immediately visible. Do not place a factory or boiler behind them and do not make a finished-goods ornament in front of a building.
Style: hand-painted vanilla-compatible technology illustration, broad readable masses, restrained matte brushed and granular textures, real volume and soft upper-left material lighting. Keep the warm-neutral style of the old icon without copying its pottery composition. Not a flat PM pictogram, glossy CGI photograph, badge or landscape. White sugar must remain genuinely near-white, pottery naturally reddish-brown; no global blue/teal cast, no sepia filter.
Background and framing: genuine transparent alpha around the whole group, in exterior gaps and visible openings not occupied by material. Square at least 1024 pixels, generous transparent margins, entire tip, base and mould intact. No floor, tabletop, ground plane, cast ground shadow, frame, circle or medallion. Only contact/object shading.
Readability: large simple conical crystal mass, one strongly contrasting mould mouth; legible at 48/64 pixels. Do not rely on tiny detailing or captions.
Historical basis: sugar was refined and crystallized into cone-shaped loaves in earthenware moulds. Represent a conceptual refinement-and-moulding group, not a certified museum replica or the older collecting-pot assembly.
Do not add sugar cubes (modern visual cue), sugar paper, sack, cane stems, sugar nippers, spoon, chunks, bowl of powder, smoke, furnace, text, labels, watermark, numbers, arrows, people, hands, ornament or modern equipment. Only the white loaf and its one matching hollow mould.
Change the sugar icon only. The separately approved forestry and hand-quern images are not input targets and must remain unmodified.
